{{Short description|Information collected from individual respondents to a survey}}
{{Other uses|Microdata (disambiguation)}}

In the study of [[Statistical survey|survey]] and census [[data]], '''microdata''' is information at the level of individual respondents.<ref name="ipums1">{{cite web |url=https://international.ipums.org/international-action/faq#ques7 |title=IPUMS-l: FAQ |publisher=IPUMS International}}</ref> For instance, a national [[census]] might collect age, home [[Address (geography)|address]], [[education]]al level, [[employment]] status, and many other variables, recorded separately for every person who responds; this is microdata.

==Advantages==
Survey/census results are most commonly published as [[aggregate data|aggregates]] (e.g. a [[region]]al-level [[employment rate]]), both for privacy reasons and because of the large quantities of data involved; microdata for one census can easily contain millions of records, each with several dozen data items.

However, summarizing results to an aggregate level results in information loss. For instance, if statistics for education and employment are aggregated separately, they cannot be used to explore a relationship between these two variables. Access to microdata allows researchers much more freedom to investigate such interactions and perform detailed analysis.<ref name="ipums1"/>

Microdata from censuses is especially useful in the evaluation of patterns of social mobility, allowing researchers to achieve more nuanced analysis than would be possible using aggregate summaries alone, and perhaps to address questions that would not have occurred to the original compilers of the data. For example, a study of social mobility in the United States 1900–1940, drawing on census data, examined how women's marriage patterns and levels of education impacted their descendants' social status.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Vickers |first=Christopher |date=2023 |title=Women and the Econometrics of Family Trees |journal=NBER Working Paper Series |volume=31598 |pages=1–55}}</ref>

==Availability==
For this reason, some statistical organizations allow access to microdata for research purposes. Controls are generally imposed to limit the risk that this data may be abused or lead to loss of privacy. For example, the [[IPUMS|Integrated Public Use Microdata Series]] requires researchers to implement security measures, avoid redistribution of microdata, use microdata only for noncommercial research/education purposes, and not make any attempt to identify the individuals recorded. Names and fine-level geographical data are removed, some data items are altered as necessary to make it impossible to identify individuals, and small ethnic categories are merged.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://international.ipums.org/international/confidentiality.html |title=IPUMSl-Confidentiality |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070823010133/http://international.ipums.org/international/confidentiality.html |archive-date=2007-08-23 |publisher=Minnesota Population Center, University of Minnesota}}</ref>

The International Household Survey Network has developed tools and guidelines to help interested  statistical agencies improve their microdata management practices. The Microdata Management Toolkit is a DDI [[metadata]] editor which is now used in about 80 countries, with the support of the Accelerated Data Program, implemented by the [[PARIS21]] Secretariat, the [[World Bank]], and other partners, in the context of the Marrakech Action Plan for Statistics.
